title-group.article-title: HDAC inhibitor tucidinostat and metronomic capecitabine plus endocrine therapy for patients with HR-positive HER2-negative advanced breast cancer after CDK4/6 inhibitors treatment: clinical findings and exploratory circulating tumor cell and ctDNA biomarker analyses of a multicenter, phase 2 study (SYSUCC-020 trial)

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Treatment options for patients with hormone receptor (HR)-positive, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative advanced breast cancer (ABC) that progresses after CDK4/6 inhibitor (CDK4/6i) continue to evolve, and no single regimen has been established as the preferred standard of care. We conducted a phase 2 trial (SYSUCC-020, NCT05411380) to investigate the efficacy and safety of a novel combination of tucidinostat and metronomic capecitabine (mCAP) with endocrine therapy (ET) in patients following progression on CDK4/6i. This trial adopted a Simon two-stage design: eligible patients received tucidinostat plus metronomic capecitabine together with either an aromatase inhibitor (Cohort 1) or fulvestrant (Cohort 2), selected according to prior ET. Seventy-two female patients were screened and sixty-six patients were included in the efficacy and safety analyses. The median follow-up was 13.88 months (Interquartile range, 8.67–20.67) and the objective response rate was 25.8%, with 17 partial responses. The median progression-free survival (PFS) was 5.39 months (95% CI, 4.07–7.69), namely 6.93 months (95% CI, 4.76–12.22) in Cohort 1 and 3.98 months (95% CI, 2.79–7.59) in Cohort 2. Most patients (93.9%) experienced at least one adverse event. In addition, exploratory analyses of biomarkers indicated that the baseline TP53 mutation status (Wild type vs. mutated, 7.64 months vs. 3.55 months) and circulating tumor cell (CTC) status (CTC-negative vs. CTC-positive, 7.59 months vs. 3.78 months) were associated with the median PFS. Our study demonstrated that tucidinostat combined with mCAP and ET is efficacious and well-tolerated in patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC previously treated with CDK4/6i.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Breast cancer is the most common female cancer in the world.1 Hormone receptor (HR)-positive and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative breast cancer is the most common type, accounting for two-thirds of all breast cancers.2 Despite high endocrine responsiveness, a proportion of patients with HR-positive HER2-negative breast cancer experience distant relapse or metastasis, resulting in advanced breast cancer (ABC).3 Cyclin-dependent kinase 4 and 6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) have changed the treatment landscape and are the most common first-line treatment for HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.4 Despite the success of CDK4/6i in the adjuvant and late-stage treatment of such patients, intrinsic resistance or secondary resistance occurs in some patients during treatment, resulting in disease progression.5 However, there is still uncertainty regarding the optimal treatment for patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC after CDK4/6i failure.

Metronomic chemotherapy is characterized by the administration of low-dose and frequent cytotoxic drugs to elicit a prolonged anticancer effect, while concurrently minimizing toxicity.6 Common drugs used for metronomic chemotherapy in patients with breast cancer include capecitabine and vinorelbine.7 An observational real-world analysis, the VICTOR-6 study, demonstrated the safety and efficacy of metronomic capecitabine (mCAP)-based regimens in HR-positive HER2-negative ABC patients.8 In addition, several clinical studies have suggested the antitumor efficacy of endocrine therapy (ET) in combination with mCAP in patients with ABC.9,10 Based on these findings, we initiated the MECCA trial, a phase 3 study designed to compare mCAP plus aromatase inhibitor (AI) versus AI alone as first-line treatment in patients with HR-positive, HER2-negative ABC.11 The trial results demonstrated that the combination significantly improved both progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) compared with AI monotherapy.11

Previous studies have demonstrated that CDK4/6i mediates epigenetic modification to promote antitumor effects in patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.12,13 Epigenetic alterations can be modulated or reversed with histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, which modify the status of acetylation of histone and nonhistone proteins to affect not only cancer cells, but also the tumor microenvironment.14,15 The complex formed by HDAC1 and MTA2, which is associated with SETD6, regulates estrogen-responsive gene expression and controls the proliferation of breast carcinoma cells.16 HDAC inhibitors can enhance breast cancer cells’ sensitivity to endocrine therapy by reversing epigenetic silencing of estrogen-responsive genes and targeting non-histone proteins like AKT and HIF1α.16,17 The HDAC inhibitor, tucidinostat, also known as chidamide, has shown antitumor effects in preclinical and clinical studies.18,19 Jiang et al. reported that tucidinostat in combination with exemestane improved the PFS of patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC with acceptable toxicity.20 These findings provide a rationale for the use of a combination of an HDAC inhibitor and ET to treat patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.11

Circulating tumor cell (CTC) count and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) could provide prognostic information and act as efficacy predictive biomarkers in ABC.21,22 Elevated baseline CTC count and ctDNA level indicate greater tumor aggressiveness and often predict inferior responses to endocrine therapies in ABC.21,23 Detection of specific ctDNA mutations further enhances predictive accuracy, aiding in patient stratification for tailored treatment strategies.24,25 These baseline liquid biopsies thus provide a non-invasive approach to anticipating outcomes and guiding therapeutic selection. We evaluated the efficacy and safety of tucidinostat and mCAP with ET in patients following progression on CDK4/6i treatment. The participants were allocated to Cohort 1 (aromatase inhibitor [AI]) or Cohort 2 (fulvestrant) according to their previous ET exposure. In addition, we designed an exploratory analysis of CTC and ctDNA in most of the patients from this trial to determine the associations between CTC/ctDNA and clinical outcomes.

sec.title: Patient characteristics and trial design
sec.p: From November 2022 to January 2025, a total of 72 patients from multiple centers in China were screened. One patient did not meet the eligibility criteria and five patients (6.9%) did not receive assigned treatment or undergo efficacy assessment because of consent withdrawal (N = 3) and loss to follow-up (N = 2) (Fig. 1, Supplementary Table 1). Finally, 66 patients were included in the efficacy analysis set and safety analysis set. As of the data cutoff on January 31, 2025, the median follow-up was 13.88 months (Interquartile range, 8.67–20.67), and 16 (24.2%) patients remained under treatment. Baseline demographic characteristics were well-balanced between the two cohorts, except for the number of prior lines of treatment (Table 1). Most of the patients (72.7%) had received ≥2 prior lines of treatment. Even 83.3% patients had visceral disease, and 78.8% had ≥2 metastatic sites. The duration of treatment with prior CDK4/6i approached statistical significance between Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 (P = 0.072). In the total cohort, 11 patients (26.8%) in Cohort 1 had received prior CDK4/6i treatment for less than 12 months, while 13 patients (52.0%) in Cohort 2 progressed within 12 months of CDK4/6i treatment.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: In the first stage of Simon’s two-stage design, 12 patients were enrolled in Cohort 1, with a response rate of 33.3% (four out of 12 patients). In Cohort 2, nine patients were enrolled, yielding a response rate of 11.1% (one out of nine patients). The objective response rate (ORR) in both cohorts met the predefined criteria, thereby allowing the study to progress to the second stage. Given the relatively lower ORR observed in Cohort 2, subsequent patient enrollment was preferentially directed towards Cohort 1. Ultimately, a total of 45 patients were enrolled and 41 patients were included in efficacy analysis in Cohort 1, while 26 patients were enrolled and 25 patients were included efficacy analysis in Cohort 2.

In the efficacy analysis set, 33 patients (50.0%) showed a decrease in target lesion size from baseline (Fig. 2a). A confirmed objective response was achieved in 17 patients (25.8%; Table 2), with a median time to response of 3.61 months (95% Confidence Interval [CI], 3.55–4.69; Fig. 2b). The disease control rate (DCR) and clinical benefit rate (CBR) were 69.7% (47/66) and 43.9% (29/66), respectively. In the efficacy analysis set, the median PFS was 5.39 months (95% CI, 4.07–7.69) with 50 PFS events occurred (Fig. 2c). In a post-hoc analysis, Cohort 1 showed a median PFS of 6.93 months (95% CI, 4.76–12.22), compared with 3.98 months (95% CI, 2.79–7.59) in Cohort 2 (Hazard Ratio [HR], 1.74 [95% CI, 1.00–3.07]; P = 0.059; Fig. 2d). After adjustment for potential confounders (e.g., number of prior lines, visceral diseases, and ESR1 status), the difference remained non-significant (Supplementary Table 2). As for best overall response, 31.7% and 22.0% patients in Cohort 1 achieved partial response (PR) and progressive disease (PD), respectively, while 16.0% and 44.0% patients achieved PR and PD in Cohort 2, respectively (Fig. 2e). In the univariate analysis, none of the factors reached statistical significance, although assignment to Cohort 2 approached significance (HR = 1.71, 95% CI 0.98–3.01, P = 0.061; Supplementary Table 3).

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: In the safety analysis set, most of the patients (93.9%) showed at least one adverse event (AE) (Table 3). Grade 3–4 AEs were observed in 46.3% of Cohort 1 and 56.0% of Cohort 2 (Supplementary Table 4). The most common of AEs were neutropenia (54, 87.1%), leukopenia (48, 72.7%), anemia (37, 56.9%), thrombocytopenia (36, 54.5%), elevated aspartate aminotransferase (35, 53.0%), elevated alanine aminotransferase (32, 48.5%), and hand–foot syndrome (21, 32.8%). Grade 3 and 4 hand–foot syndrome (4.7%) was considered to be capecitabine-related, and it is known to be cumulative. Serious adverse events (SAEs) were infrequent (3.0%) and occurred at similar rates in both cohorts. Treatment was discontinued for toxicity in 36.4% of patients (Cohort 1, 29.3%; Cohort 2, 48.0%). Dose reductions prompted by toxicity were recorded in 14.6% of Cohort 1 and 4.0% of Cohort 2 (Supplementary Table 4).

sec.title: Genomic biomarkers for therapy response
sec.p: The primary objective of characterizing the genomic landscape of the patients in this trial was to explore potential biomarkers to predict therapeutic response to the triplet treatment (tucidinostat and mCAP plus ET). We used the 301-gene panel from ChosenMed to call somatic mutations in the baseline and progressive blood samples (N = 23 and 17, respectively). The most frequently mutated genes in patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC after CDK4/6i progression included PIK3CA (35%), TP53 (35%), ESR1 (26%), BRCA2 (22%), and CDK12 (22%; Supplementary Fig. 1).

Given the limited sample size for sequencing, we defined patients with a response duration of ≥6 months with the best efficacy of stable disease (SD) and those with a PR as responders. Conversely, patients with SD lasting less than 6 months and those with PD were categorized as resistant patients. Using baseline ctDNA data paired with therapy response data, we evaluated the relationship between tumor response and the most frequent somatic mutations (top 20 in the cohort) (Fig. 3a). The frequency of somatic mutations in TP53 and SETD2 was significantly increased in the resistant patients (HR = 2.49, P = 0.014; HR = 3.18, P = 0.023; respectively), whereas MSH2 (HR = 0.54, P = 0.174) showed the opposite trend. Consistently, patients with wild type TP53 could achieve 7.64 months of PFS while the median PFS of patients with mutated TP53 was 3.55 months (Supplementary Table 5). In addition, we observed that the tumor mutation burden (TMB) and tumor mutation load (TML) of baseline ctDNA were significantly higher in the resistant group compared with the response group (P = 0.014 and 0.019, respectively, Fig. 3b). Consistent with these results, both TMB and TML exhibited a significant negative correlation with PFS (R = −0.493 and −0.414, respectively; Fig. 3c). We found that the mutation rate of the TP53 pathway was 10% in the response group and 54% in the resistant group, suggesting that cases with TP53 mutations are more resistant to treatment with tucidinostat and mCAP plus ET (Fig. 3d).

sec.title: CTCs status and phenotype could be regarded as prognostic biomarkers
sec.p: Because CTC examination was optional for patients, only 42 (59.2%) baseline samples, 17 (23.9%) on-treatment samples, and 26 (36.6%) progressive blood samples were used for CTC testing. Using the BestSurvivalCuts algorithm in R, we identified that the optimal cutoff value for the baseline CTC count associated with PFS was 2. We defined CTC status as positive when the count was ≥2; otherwise, CTC status was categorized as negative. We detected ≥2 CTCs in 26 out of the 42 samples at baseline (61.9%, range: 2–67 CTCs, median = 11.5). The CTC-positive group and the CTC-negative group did not significantly differ in demographic or clinical characteristics at baseline (Supplementary Table 6). The patients in the CTC-positive group had a higher proportion of prior CDK4/6i use within 12 months, although the difference was not significant (57.7% vs. 25.0%, P = 0.080). The patients with baseline CTC-positive status (median PFS: 3.78 [2.37–5.52]) had shorter PFS compared with CTC-negative patients (median PFS: 7.59 (3.52–Not Estimable [NE])) (Table 2; Fig. 4a). The proportion of CTC-negative patients was significantly higher in the response group compared with the resistant group (55.5% vs 25.0%, P = 0.044, Fig. 4b). Furthermore, the baseline CTC count in the resistant group was higher than that in the response group (median CTC count, 3.5 vs 1.5, P = 0.119) (Fig. 4c).

sec.p: Subgroup analysis confirmed the predictive value of the baseline CTC status. In Cohort 1, CTC-negative patients (median PFS: 17.41 [17.40–NE]) had significantly longer PFS than the CTC-positive patients (median PFS: 4.76 [2.00–NE]) (Table 2; Fig. 4d). In contrast, baseline CTC status did not distinguish the PFS differences in Cohort 2 (Fig. 4e). To further explore the correlation between baseline CTC phenotype and PFS, we performed subset analysis based on four CTC markers, including BCL-2, Ki-67, estrogen receptor (ER), and HER2. Multiple subgroup analysis revealed that CTC-positive ER-positive patients had longer PFS than CTC-positive ER-negative patients (4.76 months vs 1.92 months, P = 0.081) (Fig. 4f, Table 2). Other phenotype markers did not distinguish the prognosis of patients with positive CTC status (Supplementary Fig. 2). Additionally, the analysis of baseline and on-treatment CTC status demonstrated that the ratios of ER expression in CTC increased after the triplet treatment (Fig. 4g). The analysis of 21 patients with paired baseline and after treatment CTC amounts revealed that the number of CTC amounts increased significantly after PD (Fig. 4h).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC)-020 trial demonstrates that tucidinostat and mCAP with AI or Ful is an effective and safe treatment option in patients with ER-positive HER2-negative ABC who had progressed on prior ET and CDK4/6i. The ORR and median PFS of the triplet treatment in overall population were 25.8% and 5.39 months, respectively. The benefit of PFS was observed in the Cohort 1 (median PFS: 6.93 months) and in patients with negative baseline CTC status (median PFS: 17.41 months). The triple treatment exhibited manageable toxicity with most AEs being of grade 1 or 2 severity. The most frequent grade 3 or 4 AE was neutropenia, occurring in 32.3% of patients in cohort 1 and 6.5% in cohort 2.

Resistance to ET combined with CDK4/6i is a major challenge in the treatment of HR-positive HER2-negative ABC. To overcome this challenge, continuation of CDK4/6i, co-targeting the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, novel ETs, and non-ETs have been applied and improved clinical outcomes of this population.26 In the PACE trial, the combination of Ful, Ful plus palbociclib, Ful plus palbociclib and avelumab achieved PFS of 4.8, 4.6, and 8.1 months, respectively, in ER-positive HER2-negative ABC patients who had received prior CDK4/6i and AI.27 The phase 2 BYLieve trial revealed that PI3Kα inhibitor alpelisib combined with and Ful achieved a median PFS of 8.0 months and an ORR of 23% in HR-positive HER2-negative BC patients following progression on CDK4/6i with detectable PIK3CA mutations.28 Another trial, the EMERALD trial, demonstrated that the median PFS was 2.8 months in the Elacestrant group, which was a novel oral selective estrogen receptor modulator drug.29 However, these regimens are not globally accepted as the standard of care for the CDK4/6-inhibitor-refractory population. In addition, these options are often unavailable (PIK3CA testing is not offered in many centers), impose substantial financial burden, or may cause considerable toxicity. The present study demonstrated a potential therapy with similar efficacy in patients after CDK4/6i failure— tucidinostat and mCAP with ET—which achieved the median PFS of 5.39 months and the ORR of 25.8%. For patients previously treated with CDK4/6i and Ful, the combination of ribociclib plus AI achieved a PFS of 5.36 months in ER-positive HER2-negative ABC patients.30 This study demonstrated that tucidinostat and mCAP with AI had a consistent treatment efficacy with the median PFS of 6.93 months (95% CI, 4.76–12.22) and ORR of 31.7% (Table 2).

The present study revealed that the combination of tucidinostat and mCAP in patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC achieved a higher ORR when used with AI (31.7%) compared with the combination with Ful (16.0%) (Table 2). Additionally, the patients in Cohort 2 had a higher frequency of ESR1 mutations compared with those in Cohort 1 (31% vs. 20%, Supplementary Fig. 3). ESR1 mutations have been recognized as a poor prognosis biomarker and a predictive biomarker of ET.29,31 The difference in ESR1 mutation frequency between the two cohorts may be attributed to the higher proportion of patients in Cohort 2 who had previously been treated with AI (96.0%) compared with Cohort 1 (68.3%). Prior research has reported that tucidinostat can enhance the transcription of ER and progesterone receptor.32,33 Consistent with these findings, our study demonstrated that tucidinostat promoted the expression of ER in CTCs from on-treatment blood samples (Fig. 4h).

HDACs are aberrantly recruited to ERα target genes, which can result in endocrine resistance due to the loss of any of the corepressors associated with ERα.34 Thymidine phosphorylase has been reported to predict the efficacy of capecitabine.35 Preclinical studies have established that multiple HDAC inhibitors up-regulate thymidine phosphorylase expression, providing the mechanistic rationale for combining HDAC inhibitors with mCAP.35–37 Tucidinostat in combination with AI has been approved for the treatment of HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.20 However, the efficacy of tucidinostat combined with AI in patients with prior CDK4/6i treatment remains unclear. A retrospective real-world analysis revealed the efficacy of tucidinostat combined with ET (median PFS: 2.0 months) in the treatment of patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC after the progression on CDK4/6i.38 A subgroup analysis from a phase 3 trial indicated that entinostat plus AI had a median PFS of 3.68 months in patients failed on CDK4/6i.39 In addition to HDAC inhibitors, mCAP has been widely used to treat HR-positive HER2-negative ABC patients,40,41 and recent studies demonstrate the synergic effects of the combination of mCAP and AI compared with AI alone in the first-line treatment of HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.11

The safety profile of the tucidinostat with mCAP and ET combination was consistent with that reported for HDAC inhibitors plus AI or Ful in HR-positive HER2-negative ABC.20,39 The triplet regimen was generally well-tolerated, with 33 (50%) patients experiencing grade 3 or 4 AEs and only seven (10.6%) patients experiencing grade 4 AEs. In the EMERALD trial, which enrolled a comparable population, 27.0% of patients treated with elacestrant experienced grade 3–4 AEs.29 In contrast, treatment with alpelisib in combination with fulvestrant in the SOLAR-1 trial resulted in grade 3 or 4 AEs in 78.1% of participants.42 The most common grade 3 or 4 AE was neutropenia (36.4%), with an incidence similar to the 51% reported for tucidinostat plus exemestane in the ACE trial.43 In the CDK4/6i-refractory setting, the observed incidence of grade 3–4 neutropenia (51.5%) aligns closely with rates reported for CDK4/6 inhibitor rechallenge strategies: 40% in the MAINTAIN trial, 42.4% in BioPER, and 51.0% in TRINITI-1.30,44,45 This rate of AEs may be partly due to the additional use of mCAP, which can exacerbate hematologic toxicities and hand-foot syndrome. Moreover, the triplet regimen was associated with a lower incidence of gastrointestinal AEs, gingival bleeding, and subcutaneous hemorrhage compared with other regimens of CDK4/6i and ET, suggesting an improved bleeding-safety profile.46,47

The present study explored the prognosis value of baseline ctDNA mutation and CTC status in patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC. Pascual et al. have reported a consistent finding that patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC have a detectable TP53 mutation in plasma, and this confers them a worse outcome compared with patients without TP53 mutation (median PFS 4.4 months vs. 10.9 months).23 A retrospective analysis of the PALOMA-3 study revealed that patients that had TP53 mutations exhibited poorer survival outcomes, regardless of whether they were treated with endocrine-based therapies or chemotherapy.48 These findings suggest that TP53 mutations may confer an aggressive disease behavior that is not influenced by the type of treatment administered.49 This study provided initial evidence for the use of baseline CTC status as a prognosis and predictive marker, especially in Cohort 1 (CTC-positive vs. CTC-negative, median PFS 17.41 months vs. 4.76 months). Lorenzo et al. likewise showed that baseline CTCs were strongly prognostic: Stage IV patients with low counts had a median PFS of 5.7 months versus 3.5 months for those with high counts (HR 1.69, 90% CI 1.27–2.24, P < 0.001).50 However, given the small sample size of this exploratory analysis, associations between baseline ctDNA mutations, CTC status, and treatment efficacy should be interpreted with caution.

The present study has several limitations, including the lack of a control group and a small sample size. A randomized phase 3 trial comparing this triplet regimen with standard-of-care is currently under development. However, patient allocation to Cohort 1 or Cohort 2 according to prior endocrine-therapy introduces selection bias that attenuates the validity of any efficacy comparisons of the triplet regimen between the two cohorts. Long-term follow-up is ongoing, while the OS data are not final. In addition, the biomarker analysis in this study was based on the blood samples collected at baseline, with a lack of dynamic data collection and small sample size. This approach can cause unreliable results because the enrolled patients with different baseline characteristics, various tumor responses to therapy during treatment, and the predictive value of such biomarkers may be overestimated, warranting further prospective validation.

The novel combination of tucidinostat and mCAP with ET exhibits antitumor activity and manageable toxicity as a treatment after CDK4/6i failure for patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC. Our findings support using this triplet treatment as a potential treatment option for HR-positive HER2-negative ABC, warranting further validation in large-scale phase 3 clinical trials.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: This SYSUCC-020 trial was a phase 2, multicenter, open-label study that enrolled patients with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC after progression on CDK4/6i. The inclusion criteria were as follows: female sex and age >18 years; pathologically confirmed metastatic or recurrent HR-positive HER2-negative adenocarcinoma of the breast; postmenopausal women or premenopausal women who were required to have undergone treatment with ovarian function suppression; CDK4/6i failure; received ≤ 1 chemotherapy in the metastatic stage; an eastern cooperative oncology group (ECOG) performance status of 0–1; at least one measurable lesion based on the response evaluation criteria in solid tumors (RECIST) v1.1 guidelines51; and adequate kidney, liver, cardiovascular, and bone marrow functions. CDK4/6i failure was defined as failure in either the metastatic stage or the adjuvant setting (progressed during adjuvant treatment or within 1 year after standard CDK4/6i treatment in the adjuvant setting). This study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05411380) and was initiated on October 3, 2022.

sec.title: Ethics statement
sec.p: Prior to study entry, all patients were required to provide written informed consent. The study protocol (B2022-548-Y03) was approved by the ethical and institutional review boards of all participating institutions and was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. A steering committee (Ethics Committee of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center) provided oversight for the study.

sec.title: Treatment
sec.p: The patients were assigned to receive tucidinostat (30 mg twice weekly) and mCAP (500 mg three times daily) plus AI (Cohort 1) or Ful (Cohort 2) based on their prior ET. Regarding the choice of ET, if a patient has no prior history of Ful treatment, they are assigned to Cohort 2. Conversely, if patients had previously received treatment with Ful, they were assigned to Cohort 1 to receive either steroidal or non-steroidal AIs. The selection of AI was guided by the patient’s prior exposure to AI therapy. Specifically, if a patient had previously demonstrated disease progression while on a non-steroidal AI (e.g., anastrozole or letrozole) but had not been treated with exemestane, exemestane was the preferred subsequent option. Conversely, if a patient had progressed on exemestane but had not received a non-steroidal AI, a non-steroidal AI (anastrozole or letrozole) was considered the preferred alternative.

sec.title: Assessments
sec.p: Safety was assessed in terms of AEs. Laboratory data, vital signs, and ECG changes were also assessed. AE severity was graded in line with the common terminology criteria for adverse events (CTCAE) v4.03. Objective tumor response assessment was based on RECIST v1.1 guidelines.51

sec.title: Objectives and end points
sec.p: The primary objective of this trial was to investigate the efficacy of tucidinostat and mCAP plus ET in women with HR-positive HER2-negative ABC. Secondary objective was to explore and evaluate the safety of this triplet combination therapy. The primary end point was the ORR. Secondary end points were the DCR, CBR, PFS, and safety. ORR was defined as the proportion of patients achieving complete response (CR) or PR as best overall response per RECIST v1.1. DCR was defined as the proportion of patients with best overall response of CR, PR, or SD lasting ≥6 weeks. CBR was defined as the proportion of patients with CR, PR, or SD lasting ≥24 weeks. PFS was measured from the date of treatment initiation to the date of documented disease progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first. Exploratory analysis included the determination of biomarkers of ctDNA and CTC. Safety and tolerability end points included AEs, SAEs, vital signs, and clinical chemistry and hematology parameters. Safety was monitored from baseline until 30 days (±7 days) after the last dose. Participants were assessed for AEs through both investigators questioning (at all scheduled visits) and spontaneous reporting by participants. Any AE, regardless of suspected causality, was documented in case report forms, including details on severity, relationship to the study drug, actions taken, and outcomes. Standard laboratory parameters (chemistry, ECG, tumor markers) and vital signs were measured at baseline and at each visit. Complete blood count was checked once a week. AEs were graded using the CTCAE v5.0 criteria. SAEs were defined in accordance with ICH-GCP guidelines and reported to the Institutional Review Board within 24 h. A final safety assessment was conducted at the end-of-study visit. Tumor efficacy assessments were conducted every 2 cycles until disease progression or initiation of new anti-tumor treatment.

sec.title: Sample collection, ctDNA sequencing and CTC procedures
sec.p: Briefly, 10 mL of whole blood (Streck Cell-Free DNA BCT) was collected at baseline, at the end of cycle 2 and at treatment completion (progression or toxicity withdrawal). Plasma was separated at 4 °C and used for ctDNA extraction (Concert C1101 kit) and targeted sequencing with a 301-gene panel (ChosenMed) on the MGISEQ2000, following the vendor’s QC/variant-calling pipeline (hg19, BWA/GATK/VarDict/ANNOVAR). For CTC enumeration, the same blood draw was processed through the OmiCell® microfluidic filter (Anfang Biotech); cells were stained and scored for ER, HER2, BCL-2 and Ki67. CTC positivity was defined as ≥2 cells, and each marker was considered positive if ≥1 cell expressed it. Further procedural details and the determination of cut-off values or CTC positivity are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: This study compared the investigator-assessed ORR of patients treated with tucidinostat and mCAP plus AI or Ful. The ORR for the Cohort 1 was expected to be 14% with tucidinostat and AI, while the combination regimen with mCAP was expected to increase the ORR to 35%.20 A one-sided type I error rate (α) of 0.05 and a power (1−β) of 0.80 were set for this study. The Simon’s two-stage optimal design was used for sample-size calculation. In the first stage, 12 patients were included. If there was more than two patient who responded to the triplet treatment, the study would proceed to the second stage with a total enrollment of 31 patients. Assuming a dropout rate of 10%, a total of 35 patients were required for enrollment.

The ORR for Cohort 2 was expected to be 15% with tucidinostat and Ful, while the combination regimen with mCAP was expected to increase the ORR to 35%. A one-sided type I error rate (α) of 0.05 and a power (1−β) of 0.80 were set for this study. The Simon’s two-stage optimal design was used for sample-size calculation. In the first stage, nine patients were included. If one or more patients responded to the triplet treatment, the study would proceed to the second stage, with a total enrollment of 34 patients. Assuming a dropout rate of 10%, a total of 38 patients were required for enrollment.

The primary efficacy analysis set comprised participants with both a baseline and at least one post-baseline efficacy assessment. Safety was analyzed in the safety analysis set who had received at least one dose of the study medication. Cumulative survival rates were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method and compared via the stratified log-rank test in the full analysis set, which included all randomly assigned patients except those who either declined to initiate protocol-specified treatment or had no post-randomization follow-up records. The proportional hazards assumption for PFS was assessed and confirmed using Schoenfeld residuals. Subgroup analyses were conducted according to key baseline clinical-pathological factors. Exploratory biomarker analysis was performed using a nonparametric method. Statistical analyses were conducted using R (version 3.6.3).
